title: Why Does the Scrotum Tighten During Winter and Become Loose During Summer?

Introduction

Many men notice that the scrotum becomes tight, wrinkled, and elevated during cold weather but appears loose and hangs lower during warm weather. This change is completely normal and represents one of the body’s important thermoregulatory mechanisms. The primary function of the scrotum is not simply to support the testes, but to maintain them at an optimal temperature required for normal sperm production and reproductive function.

Why Are the Testes Located Outside the Body?

Unlike most organs, the testes are located within the scrotum outside the abdominal cavity. This unique anatomical arrangement is essential because sperm production (spermatogenesis) requires a temperature that is lower than the body’s core temperature. If the testes remain too warm for prolonged periods, sperm production and sperm quality may be adversely affected.

The scrotum therefore acts as a natural temperature-regulating organ, continuously adjusting the position of the testes and the characteristics of the scrotal skin to maintain an environment that supports normal reproductive function.

What Happens During Cold Weather?

When the surrounding temperature decreases, temperature-sensitive receptors in the scrotal skin activate reflexes that help conserve heat.

The dartos muscle, located within the scrotal wall, contracts, causing the scrotal skin to become tight and wrinkled. This reduces the surface area of the scrotum, minimizing heat loss to the environment.

At the same time, the cremaster muscle contracts and gently pulls the testes closer to the body, where they are exposed to warmer temperatures. Together, these coordinated responses help preserve the optimal temperature necessary for normal sperm production.

The cremaster muscle may also contract during emotional stress, fear, anxiety, or sudden stimulation because of increased sympathetic nervous system activity.

What Happens During Hot Weather?

In warm environments, the opposite response occurs.

The dartos and cremaster muscles relax, allowing the scrotum to become loose and the testes to hang farther away from the body. This increases the exposed surface area and promotes heat dissipation.

Sweat glands within the scrotal skin also become more active, and evaporation of sweat helps cool the testes. Increased blood flow to the scrotal skin further enhances heat exchange with the surrounding environment.

These coordinated physiological mechanisms help maintain a stable testicular temperature despite changes in environmental conditions.

What Happens During Exercise?

During vigorous physical activity, temporary contraction of the cremaster muscle may briefly elevate the testes because of increased sympathetic nervous system activity. As exercise continues, thermoregulatory mechanisms become more prominent, allowing heat to dissipate and helping maintain an appropriate testicular temperature.

Recent human research has shown that scrotal temperature changes dynamically during running, highlighting the importance of continuous thermoregulation in protecting testicular function during physical activity.

Conclusion

The tightening of the scrotum during cold weather and its relaxation during warm weather are normal physiological adaptations designed to regulate testicular temperature. Through the coordinated actions of the dartos muscle, cremaster muscle, sweat glands, and local blood vessels, the scrotum continuously protects the testes from excessive heat or cold, helping preserve normal sperm production and male fertility. These changes are an essential part of healthy reproductive physiology and should be regarded as a normal function of the human body.

References

2. Scientific Reports (Nature): Scrotal temperature change during running in humans. 2025.
